findings.claim: The 2024 examiners’ report highlighted OSI layer descriptions as a weak area — students could name layers but not describe what each one does.
findings.truth: No such report is cited or verifiable. The spec prints no examiner commentary and no question ladder. The teaching point (students name layers but cannot describe them) is sound, so keep the point and drop the invented source.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/computer-science-C500QS.md lines 245-256 give only the assessment facts (written examination 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 50%); the spec contains no examiners' report. Fabricated source.

findings.claim: Routing cost calculation is an Eduqas-specific topic that other boards do not assess.
findings.truth: Student-facing prose must never name the board. The spec does list 'methods of routing traffic on a network and calculation of routing costs', so the topic is directly examinable; the comparative claim about other boards is unverifiable and unnecessary.
findings.evidence: House rule for this board; spec line 442 lists routing cost calculation as required content.

findings.claim: The seven main threats you must know are: malware (malicious software), phishing/social engineering (psychological deception), brute-force attacks (exhaustive password guessing), DoS/DDoS (flooding a server), data interception (capturing network traffic), and SQL injection (manipulating database queries via input fields).
findings.truth: The sentence says seven but lists only six items, because phishing and social engineering are merged. The spec names seven separate threats: malware, phishing, social engineering, brute force attacks, denial of service attacks, data interception and theft, SQL injection. The revision tip on the same block already lists all seven.
findings.evidence: Spec lines 471-479 list the seven threats; internal count of the sentence gives six.

findings.claim: Protocol: https [0.5] / Path: /revision/networks [0.5] — award 1 mark if both correct. Accept https:// for protocol.
findings.truth: GCSE marks are whole numbers; half marks do not exist. The mark scheme should state that both parts are needed for the single mark, without inventing half marks.
findings.evidence: spec lines 245-253 (100 marks and 80 marks, whole-mark components); no half-mark scheme exists at GCSE.

findings.claim: Misconception 3: 'Encryption happens at the Application layer.' Encryption is primarily a Presentation layer function (layer 6). TLS/SSL, used for HTTPS, is a Presentation layer service even though it is triggered by an Application layer protocol.
findings.truth: In the real protocol stack TLS sits between the Transport and Application layers and is not a clean Presentation layer service; different sources map it to layer 5 or 6. The lesson's mapping matches standard GCSE teaching for the 7-layer model, but calling the opposite view a 'misconception' over-claims. Options: (a) leave, because the mapping matches the taught model and mark schemes; (b) soften 'is a Presentation layer service' to 'is usually placed at the Presentation layer'.
findings.evidence: OSI 7-layer model as taught in the spec (line 426); TLS is not defined by the OSI standard.
findings.ruling: NOTE: TLS at layer 6 matches the 7-layer model this spec teaches and standard classroom resources; left.

findings.claim: Mark scheme for the P-to-T routing question lists three routes: P-Q-T (8), P-R-Q-T (6), P-R-S-T (8).
findings.truth: Recomputed: all three sums are correct and 6 is the lowest, so the answer key is right. If the links are bidirectional a fourth route exists, P-Q-R-S-T = 5+1+4+2 = 12, which the scheme does not list. The chosen route is unaffected.
findings.evidence: Recomputation from the link costs given in the question.

findings.claim: Most packets carry between 500 and 1,500 bytes of payload data.
findings.truth: Loose. On Ethernet the whole IP packet is capped at 1500 bytes, so the payload is smaller than that, and real traffic is bimodal (many very small packets plus many full-size ones). Not mark-affecting at GCSE.

findings.claim: The TLD (.co.uk) indicates a commercial UK site; the TLD server handles all domains ending in .co.uk, .com and so on.
findings.truth: Strictly, .uk is the top-level domain and .co.uk is a second-level domain within it. Every GCSE resource and the spec's own vocabulary treat .co.uk as the TLD, so correcting this would contradict what teachers and mark schemes say. Recommend leave.
findings.evidence: DNS naming hierarchy; spec line 468 asks only for 'the structure of URLs'.

findings.claim: Exam tips across lessons 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 make tariff and examiner claims: 'Six-mark compare questions reward explicit contrasting language'; 'examiners reward multi-dimensional comparisons'; 'DNS resolution is a common 3-4 mark describe question'; 'Generic answers ... score no marks'.
findings.truth: The spec prints no question ladder, so none of these tariffs can be confirmed or refuted. None contradicts the assessment facts (written examination 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 50%; on-screen examination 2 hours, 80 marks, 50%), and none is impossible, so they are recorded rather than fixed. Only the lesson 3 claim cites an invented source, and that is fixed as F1.

findings.claim: Firewalls are the first line of defence against DoS attacks and many forms of intrusion.
findings.truth: A firewall alone cannot absorb a large volumetric DDoS attack; upstream rate limiting and cloud mitigation do that work. The lesson's own threat-to-defence table already lists rate limiting and cloud-based mitigation alongside the firewall, so the point is not left bare. Not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: Spec line 493 lists firewalls as a protection method without ranking them; internal consistency with the lesson table.

summary: Technical content is accurate: OSI layer order and numbering, protocol-to-layer mapping, TCP vs UDP, hub/switch/router behaviour, 48-bit MAC, worm vs virus, DNS resolution order and all five knowledge-check answer keys per lesson check out, and both routing-cost worked examples recompute correctly (6 in each). Four fixes: one fabricated examiners' report citation, one board name in student prose, one 'seven threats' sentence that lists six, and one half-mark mark scheme.
